title: Coronary Artery Disease & Acute Coronary Syndrome: Ischemia Recognition, Reperfusion and Complication Rescue
html:
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is a time-sensitive spectrum that includes unstable angina, non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The RN does not wait for a perfect symptom description or a final diagnosis before beginning protocol-directed assessment. The priority is to recognize possible myocardial ischemia, support oxygen delivery and perfusion, obtain diagnostic evidence quickly, activate the appropriate pathway, and watch for lethal complications.

Learning goals

  • Connect coronary atherosclerosis, plaque disruption, thrombosis, ischemia, and myocardial injury.
  • Recognize both classic and less typical ACS presentations without relying on stereotypes.
  • Prioritize ECG acquisition, serial biomarkers, monitoring, and rapid team activation.
  • Differentiate the nursing implications of STEMI, NSTEMI, and unstable angina.
  • Administer antiplatelet, anticoagulant, nitrate, oxygen, and reperfusion therapies safely.
  • Detect dysrhythmias, heart failure, shock, bleeding, and mechanical complications early.

Ischemia is a time-sensitive oxygen imbalance

Coronary artery disease usually develops as atherosclerotic plaque narrows or destabilizes a coronary artery. When plaque ruptures or erodes, platelet activation and thrombus formation can abruptly reduce blood flow. Myocardial ischemia occurs when oxygen supply cannot meet demand. Prolonged severe ischemia causes irreversible myocardial injury and releases cardiac troponin.

Stable angina is generally predictable with exertion or stress and improves with rest or prescribed therapy. New, worsening, prolonged, or rest symptoms raise concern for ACS. NSTEMI and STEMI both involve myocardial injury; the initial ECG pattern and coronary occlusion pathway guide urgency and treatment. Unstable angina may cause ischemic symptoms without a diagnostic troponin rise, but still requires urgent risk assessment.

Recognize the whole presentation

Possible ischemic symptoms include central pressure, squeezing, heaviness, fullness, burning, or pain; discomfort in an arm, shoulder, back, neck, jaw, or upper abdomen; dyspnea; diaphoresis; nausea; vomiting; palpitations; lightheadedness; syncope; or unusual fatigue. Symptoms may be intense or mild, sudden or gradual, continuous or intermittent.

Older adults, women, and clients with diabetes, kidney disease, cognitive impairment, or prior cardiac disease may present with prominent dyspnea, weakness, nausea, confusion, or fatigue. These patterns do not exclude chest discomfort, and demographic assumptions must never replace assessment. Ask about onset, provocation, quality, radiation, severity, duration, recurrence, associated symptoms, activity, prior episodes, cardiac history, medications, and what has already been taken.

Treat the risk, not the vocabulary
A client does not need to say “chest pain” to have ACS. New unexplained pressure, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, syncope, or severe fatigue can justify immediate evaluation.

First minutes: stabilize and gather decisive data

Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, skin, pain or discomfort, vital signs, oxygen saturation, perfusion, and signs of heart failure or shock. Stop exertion, place the client at rest, obtain emergency assistance according to setting, establish continuous cardiac monitoring, secure IV access, and obtain a 12-lead ECG rapidly under the ACS pathway. Do not allow routine paperwork or a chest radiograph to delay ECG or reperfusion activation.

If the first ECG is nondiagnostic but symptoms continue or recur, report the change and anticipate serial ECGs or additional leads. Compare with prior tracings when available, but do not dismiss a new concerning pattern because a baseline abnormality exists. A monitor rhythm strip helps identify dysrhythmias; it does not replace a diagnostic 12-lead ECG.

A normal first test does not close the case

High-sensitivity cardiac troponin is interpreted as a serial trend with symptom timing, ECG, examination, and clinical probability. An early result can be normal before injury is detectable. An elevated troponin indicates myocardial injury but is not specific to plaque rupture; sepsis, tachydysrhythmia, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, kidney disease, myocarditis, and other conditions can also elevate it.

Draw ordered laboratory studies without delaying emergency therapy. Common data include serial troponin, complete blood count, electrolytes, glucose, kidney function, coagulation studies, and lipid testing. Chest imaging or echocardiography may clarify alternative diagnoses, wall-motion abnormalities, ventricular function, or complications. Continue to evaluate other lethal causes of chest symptoms, including aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, esophageal rupture, and pericardial tamponade.

Immediate medications require screening

Protocol-directed chewable aspirin is commonly given promptly when ACS is suspected unless allergy, active major bleeding, or another contraindication exists. Verify what the client already took and document dose and time. Additional P2Y12 antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy depends on the ACS and reperfusion plan, bleeding risk, kidney function, body weight, procedures, and authorized orders.

Nitroglycerin can reduce ischemic discomfort and cardiac workload, but assess blood pressure, hemodynamic stability, right-ventricular involvement, recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use, and other contraindications first. Relief after nitroglycerin does not prove a cardiac cause, and lack of relief does not exclude MI. Opioids are not a substitute for reperfusion and may complicate assessment; follow the current pathway.

Oxygen is a treatment for hypoxemia

Give supplemental oxygen for hypoxemia, respiratory distress, or another clinical indication and titrate to the ordered target. Routine oxygen for every client with suspected ACS and normal oxygenation is not benign or evidence based. Position the client to support breathing while considering blood pressure and perfusion, and reassess after every intervention.

Reperfusion is the priority in STEMI

A diagnostic STEMI pattern with a compatible presentation triggers immediate reperfusion activation. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is preferred when it can be delivered within the system's target. If timely PCI is unavailable, an eligible client may receive fibrinolytic therapy under a defined pathway followed by transfer and reassessment. The RN communicates symptom onset and ECG time, minimizes avoidable delay, maintains monitoring and access, prepares for transport or the catheterization laboratory, and documents key milestones.

Before fibrinolysis, screen carefully for contraindications such as prior intracranial hemorrhage, active bleeding, suspected aortic dissection, recent major trauma or surgery, severe uncontrolled hypertension, and other protocol-defined risks. After administration, monitor neurologic status, bleeding, perfusion, rhythm, pain, and ECG response. Sudden headache, neurologic deficit, hypotension, or uncontrolled bleeding requires immediate escalation.

NSTEMI is urgent but not treated with fibrinolysis

NSTEMI management generally includes antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, anti-ischemic care, high-intensity lipid-lowering therapy, risk stratification, and an invasive strategy based on instability and risk. Fibrinolytic drugs are not used simply because troponin is elevated without STEMI criteria. Recurrent symptoms, dynamic ECG changes, heart failure, dysrhythmia, or hemodynamic instability demand urgent escalation and may accelerate angiography.

Antithrombotic therapy: prevent clot, detect bleeding

Verify allergies, current antiplatelets and anticoagulants, last doses, recent procedures, bleeding history, stroke history, pregnancy status when relevant, weight, kidney and liver function, hemoglobin, platelets, and ordered coagulation monitoring. Avoid unnecessary intramuscular injections and trauma, apply appropriate pressure after puncture, inspect urine and stool, and assess skin, gums, access sites, mentation, hemoglobin, and hemodynamics.

After ACS or coronary stenting, dual antiplatelet therapy is often essential to prevent recurrent thrombosis. Duration and drug selection are individualized to ischemic and bleeding risk. Teach clients never to stop an antiplatelet medicine on their own, including before dental or surgical care; the prescribing cardiology team must coordinate changes.

PCI care extends beyond the coronary artery

Before PCI, verify identity, procedure, consent process, allergies, renal function, antithrombotic therapy, access, baseline pulses and neurovascular status, and readiness for emergency support. After PCI, monitor rhythm, symptoms, vital signs, perfusion, the radial or femoral access site, distal circulation, and ordered activity restrictions. Track urine and kidney function when contrast exposure is relevant.

Visible access-site bleeding requires immediate pressure and help. After femoral access, new back or flank pain, hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, restlessness, or falling hemoglobin can signal retroperitoneal hemorrhage even when the groin looks dry. After radial access, monitor hand color, warmth, sensation, movement, pulse or device-directed perfusion checks, and compartment symptoms.

Right-ventricular infarction can be preload dependent

Inferior MI with hypotension, jugular venous distention, and relatively clear lungs suggests right-ventricular involvement. Reduced right-sided output limits left-ventricular filling. Nitrates, diuretics, or excessive positive pressure can worsen hypotension in a preload-dependent client. Report the pattern immediately, obtain right-sided leads if ordered, maintain close hemodynamic monitoring, and follow the individualized fluid and reperfusion plan rather than treating every infarction identically.

Watch for electrical and pump failure

Ischemic myocardium can produce premature beats, bradycardia, atrioventricular block, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, or cardiac arrest. Keep defibrillation and emergency support available, correct reversible causes, and respond to the client's perfusion—not merely the monitor number.

Acute left-ventricular failure may present with dyspnea, crackles, hypoxemia, new S3, frothy sputum, or rising work of breathing. Cardiogenic shock may cause hypotension, cool clammy skin, weak pulses, altered mentation, oliguria, rising lactate, and pulmonary congestion. Activate emergency support, optimize oxygenation and perfusion, prepare ordered vasoactive or mechanical support, and expedite revascularization. Repeated indiscriminate fluid boluses can worsen pulmonary edema.

Watch for mechanical complications

A new loud systolic murmur, abrupt pulmonary edema, recurrent chest pain, sudden hypotension, jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds, or electromechanical instability after MI can indicate papillary-muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal rupture, free-wall rupture with tamponade, or reinfarction. These are surgical or interventional emergencies. Escalate immediately and prepare for echocardiography and advanced support.

Post-MI pericardial inflammation may cause sharp positional pain and a friction rub, but recurrent ischemia and other emergencies must be excluded. Never normalize new symptoms because the client has “already had the heart attack.”

Recovery begins before discharge

Secondary prevention includes individualized antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin therapy, cardiac rehabilitation referral, tobacco cessation, blood-pressure and diabetes management, activity progression, nutrition support, psychosocial assessment, and follow-up. Medication teaching should cover purpose, schedule, bleeding precautions, adverse effects, refill access, and what to do before another procedure.

Teach the client and family to call emergency medical services for recurrent warning symptoms rather than driving. Use teach-back for the emergency plan, nitroglycerin instructions, medication adherence, access-site care, activity limits, and follow-up. Explore cost, transportation, language, caregiving, and health-literacy barriers before labeling nonadherence.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Gather symptom pattern and onset, associated symptoms, vital signs, oxygenation, perfusion, ECG, troponin trend, rhythm, medications, bleeding risks, and cardiac history.
  2. Analyze cues: Link ischemic symptoms with dynamic ECG or biomarker change while considering other lethal causes and conditions that elevate troponin.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: STEMI requiring reperfusion, unstable NSTEMI, ventricular dysrhythmia, acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock, major bleeding, and mechanical rupture outrank routine comfort needs.
  4. Generate solutions: Activate the ACS pathway, support ABCs, obtain serial diagnostic data, prepare appropriate antithrombotic and reperfusion therapy, and anticipate rescue resources.
  5. Take action: Reduce delay, verify contraindications, give protocol-directed therapy safely, monitor continuously, and escalate new instability or bleeding.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess symptoms, ECG, rhythm, oxygenation, perfusion, mental status, urine, access site, bleeding, biomarkers, and response to reperfusion and medication.

Clinical example

A client reports nausea, diaphoresis, and heavy upper-back pressure. The first troponin is within the reference range, but the symptoms began 30 minutes ago. The RN keeps the client monitored, obtains the rapid 12-lead ECG, communicates the onset time and high-risk presentation, and follows the serial ECG and troponin pathway rather than reassuring the client from one early result. When new ST elevation appears, the RN activates the STEMI pathway and prepares for urgent PCI.

Original educational synthesis. ACS diagnosis, ECG interpretation, medication selection and dose, oxygen targets, antithrombotic therapy, reperfusion eligibility and timing, fibrinolytic contraindications, PCI care, and emergency treatment require current clinical data, authorized orders, local protocols, specialist input, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official ACC, AHA, or NCSBN product.
